stimuli.text: Researchers want to investigate whether a brief mindfulness exercise before tests improves scores. They have 80 students in a statistics class available.

Random samples of 15 were taken from two groups. The values of commute time (minutes) are:

**City A:** 10, 12, 12, 15, 15, 16, 19, 19, 20, 21, 21, 23, 25, 28, 30

**City B:** 23, 23, 25, 25, 28, 28, 28, 30, 33, 36, 36, 36, 40, 44, 60
A school district claims that 60% of its students take public transit to school. A reporter suspects the true proportion is lower. In a random sample of 160 students, 91 take public transit.

Data were collected on outdoor temperature (°F) (x) and daily iced-drink sales (y) for a sample of days. A scatterplot shows a linear pattern, and the residual plot shows no pattern. Computer output for the least-squares regression is shown.

```text
Predictor   Coef      SE Coef
Constant    39.1
x           1.9
S = 5.2    R-Sq = 71.0%
```

questions.stem: The regression line is ŷ = 13 − 2.2x. An observation has x = 19 and y = -23.4. What is its residual, and what does it mean?

options.text: 5.4; the actual value is above the predicted value
options.why: Correct. Residual = y − ŷ.

options.text: 5.4; the actual value is below the predicted value
options.why: A positive residual means the point is above the line.
That is the predicted value ŷ.

options.text: -5.4; the actual value is below the predicted value
options.why: Residual = actual − predicted, not predicted − actual.

questions.stem: For a distribution of time spent on homework, the mean is 32 and the median is 41. Which is the most likely shape?

options.why: The mean is pulled toward the tail.
A uniform distribution is symmetric, with mean near the median.
Correct. A long left tail pulls the mean below the median.
In a symmetric distribution, the mean and median are close.

questions.explanation: Mean 32 < median 41: the mean is pulled toward the left tail.

questions.stem: The correlation between car age and resale price is r = 0.8. Which is a correct interpretation of r²?

options.text: About 64% of the variation in resale price is accounted for by the linear model relating resale price to car age
options.why: Correct. r² is the proportion of variation in y explained by the linear model.

options.text: Car age causes 64% of resale price
options.why: Regression does not establish causation.

options.text: About 80% of the variation in resale price is accounted for by the model
options.why: Square r.

options.text: About 64% of the predictions are correct
options.why: r² is about variation explained, not accuracy of individual predictions.

questions.stem: If the sample size quadruples, what happens to the standard deviation of the sampling distribution of x̄?

options.text: It is cut to one quarter
options.why: It depends on √n.
Correct. σ/√n: √4 = 2.
It depends on n.
Larger samples reduce variability.

questions.stem: A variable is approximately normal with mean 79 and standard deviation 13. What value is at the 10th percentile?

options.why: Correct. z = invNorm(0.1) ≈ -1.282; x = μ + zσ.
Multiply z by σ, not σ².
Use the z-score for the percentile, not the percentile itself.
Check the sign of z.

questions.stem: Does increasing the sample size reduce bias in a survey?

options.text: Yes; large samples are always unbiased
options.why: A biased method stays biased.

options.text: No; a larger sample reduces variability but not bias from the sampling method
options.why: Correct. Bias is systematic.

options.text: Yes, if the sample is over 1,000
options.why: Size does not fix a biased method.
Size never fixes bias.

questions.stem: For a distribution of household incomes in a city, the mean is 72 and the median is 83. Which is the most likely shape?

options.why: In a symmetric distribution, the mean and median are close.
A uniform distribution is symmetric, with mean near the median.
Correct. A long left tail pulls the mean below the median.
The mean is pulled toward the tail.

questions.explanation: Mean 72 < median 83: the mean is pulled toward the left tail.

questions.stem: A student is chosen at random from those who drive to school. What is the probability the student is a junior?

options.why: Correct. P(junior | drives) = juniors who drive ÷ all who drive.
That is P(drives | junior).
That is P(junior) overall.
That is P(junior and drives); divide by drivers only.

questions.stem: In a random sample of 320 students at a large high school, 112 have a part-time job. Which is a 95% confidence interval for the proportion of all students at a large high school who have a part-time job?

options.why: Multiply the standard error by z*.
Use the standard error, √(p̂(1 − p̂)/n).
Divide by n inside the square root.
Correct. p̂ ± z*√(p̂(1 − p̂)/n) with z* = 1.96.

questions.stem: A point with an x value far from the others noticeably changes the slope when removed. What is it?

options.why: The line always passes through it.

options.text: A point with a residual of 0
options.why: Influence is about leverage, not residual size.
That is a variable, not a point.
Correct. Removing it changes the regression line substantially.

questions.explanation: Removing it changes the regression line substantially.

questions.stem: Which change increases the power of a significance test, with everything else unchanged?

options.why: That lowers power.
That lowers power.

options.text: Using a two-sided instead of a one-sided test
options.why: For the correct direction, that lowers power.
Correct. Larger samples detect real effects more often.

questions.explanation: Larger samples detect real effects more often.

questions.stem: Two independent random samples have n₁ = 30, s₁ = 7 and n₂ = 19, s₂ = 6. What is the standard error of x̄₁ − x̄₂?

options.why: Correct. √(s₁²/n₁ + s₂²/n₂).
Variances add, even for a difference.
Add variances, then take the square root; standard errors do not add.
Each sample contributes s²/n.

questions.stem: A 95% confidence interval for p is (0.42, 0.51). Which claim is supported?

options.text: It is plausible that fewer than half the population has the trait
options.why: Correct. Values below 0.5 lie in the interval.

options.text: Exactly 46.5% of the population has the trait
options.why: The center is an estimate.

options.text: The population proportion must be greater than 0.5
options.why: Most of the interval is below 0.5.

options.text: There is a 95% probability that p is between 0.42 and 0.51
options.why: The probability statement applies to the method, not this interval.

questions.explanation: Values below 0.5 lie in the interval.

questions.stem: A principal divides students by grade level and takes a simple random sample of 25 students from each grade. What sampling method is this?

options.why: That selects every kth individual.
The selection is random.
Cluster sampling selects whole groups.
Correct. SRSs within groups (strata).

questions.stem: A random sample of 18 has mean 38.7 and standard deviation 14.2. Which is a 95% confidence interval for the population mean?

options.why: Divide by √n, not n.
With s estimating σ, use t*, not z*.

questions.stem: Each of 7 independent devices fails with probability 0.08. What is the probability that at least one fails?

options.why: Correct. 1 − P(none fail) = 1 − (1 − p)^n.
Probabilities of overlapping events cannot simply be added.
That is the probability all fail.
That is the probability none fail.

questions.stem: P(A) = 0.2, P(B) = 0.6 and P(A and B) = 0.16. What is P(A or B), and are A and B independent?

options.why: P(A and B) is not 0, so they are not mutually exclusive.
Correct. P(A or B) = P(A) + P(B) − P(A and B); independent if P(A and B) = P(A)P(B) = 0.12.
Compare P(A and B) with P(A)·P(B) = 0.12.
Subtract P(A and B) so the overlap is not counted twice.

questions.stem: What is the expected value of X?

options.why: That is the largest probability, not the mean.
That is the most likely value (mode), not the mean.
Correct. μ = Σ x·P(x).
Weight each value by its probability.

questions.stem: What does '95% confident' mean for a confidence interval?

options.text: In many repeated samples, about 95% of intervals built this way would capture the true parameter
options.why: Correct. Confidence describes the method's long-run success rate.

options.text: 95% of samples will have the same p̂
options.why: Sample proportions vary.

options.text: 95% of the data fall within the interval
options.why: Intervals estimate a parameter, not the data's spread.

options.text: The parameter is in this interval with probability 0.95
options.why: The parameter is fixed; it is in or not.

questions.explanation: Confidence describes the method's long-run success rate.

questions.stem: The data are: 12, 14, 17, 18, 19, 19, 23, 25, 34, 72. Using the 1.5 × IQR rule, which statement is correct?

options.why: That is the observed count.

questions.stem: What is the smallest sample size needed to estimate a proportion with a margin of error of at most 0.05 at 95% confidence, with no prior estimate of p?

questions.stem: In a randomized experiment, 138 of 230 subjects improved with treatment 1 and 61 of 180 improved with treatment 2. For a test of H₀: p₁ − p₂ = 0, what is the test statistic?

options.why: Divide the difference by its standard error.
The test uses the pooled proportion, because H₀ assumes p₁ = p₂.
Correct. Pooled p̂c = 0.4854; z = (p̂₁ − p̂₂)/√(p̂c(1 − p̂c)(1/n₁ + 1/n₂)).
Use (1/n₁ + 1/n₂).

parts.prompt: Write an investigative question for this study, and identify the explanatory and response variables.

rubric.criterion: A clear investigative question that names the population or units and the variables.
rubric.example: "Does the mindfulness exercise lead to a better score on the next unit test than a reading break for units like these?"
Explanatory: treatment (the mindfulness exercise vs a reading break). Response: score on the next unit test.

parts.prompt: Explain why an experiment, rather than an observational study, should be used to answer the question.

rubric.criterion: Only random assignment allows a cause-and-effect conclusion; an observational study could be confounded.
rubric.example: Units that choose a treatment may differ in other ways that affect the response.

parts.prompt: Describe how to randomly assign the 80 units to the two treatments in a completely randomized design.

rubric.example: Number units 1–80; use a random number generator to select 40 different numbers.
Those 40 receive the mindfulness exercise; the remaining 40 receive a reading break.

parts.prompt: The researchers consider blocking by previous test average (high or low). Explain how blocking would be carried out and why it could improve the experiment.

rubric.criterion: Form blocks and randomize within each block.
rubric.example: Separate units into the blocks, then randomly assign half of each block to each treatment.

rubric.criterion: Benefit: reduces variability in the response due to the blocking variable, making a treatment effect easier to detect.
rubric.example: Accounts for differences caused by previous test average.

parts.prompt: Find the five-number summary for each group.
Use the 1.5 × IQR rule to determine whether City B has any outliers. Show your work.

rubric.example: IQR = 11; upper fence = 36 + 1.5(11) = 52.5. Outlier(s): 60.

parts.prompt: Compare the distributions of the two groups (shape, center and variability) in context.

rubric.example: The median for City B (30) is greater than for City A (19).
City B is more variable (IQR 11 vs 8).

rubric.criterion: Comments on shape or unusual features.
rubric.example: City B has a high outlier, suggesting right skew.

parts.prompt: Which measure of center is more appropriate for City B, the mean or the median? Explain.

rubric.criterion: Median, because it is resistant to the outlier or skew.
rubric.example: Mean 33 is pulled toward the high value; median 30 is not.

parts.prompt: State the hypotheses, defining the parameter.

rubric.criterion: Correct hypotheses with the parameter defined.
rubric.example: H₀: p = 0.6; Hₐ: p < 0.6, where p is the proportion of all district students who take public transit.

parts.prompt: Identify the appropriate procedure and check its conditions.

rubric.criterion: One-sample z test for a proportion.
rubric.example: Random sample stated.
160 is less than 10% of all students (assumed); np₀ = 96 and n(1 − p₀) = 64 are both at least 10.

parts.prompt: Calculate the test statistic and p-value.
State a conclusion in context at α = 0.05.

rubric.criterion: Correct decision linked to the p-value, in context.
rubric.example: Because 0.2099 is greater than 0.05, fail to reject H₀: not convincing evidence that the proportion is less than 0.6.

parts.prompt: Write the equation of the least-squares regression line, defining the variables.

rubric.example: ŷ = 39.1 + 1.9x, where ŷ is predicted daily iced-drink sales and x is outdoor temperature (°F).

parts.prompt: Interpret the slope and the value of R-Sq in context.

rubric.example: For each additional unit of outdoor temperature (°F), the predicted daily iced-drink sales increases by about 1.9.
About 71.0% of the variation in daily iced-drink sales is accounted for by the linear model with outdoor temperature (°F).

parts.prompt: One observation has x = 3 and y = 41.5. Calculate and interpret its residual. Also find the correlation r.

rubric.example: ŷ = 44.8; residual = 41.5 − 44.8 = -3.3: the actual value is below the prediction.

parts.prompt: The data come from a convenience sample. Explain how this affects the conclusions and describe a better data collection method.

rubric.criterion: Results may not generalize to the population; a random sample would allow generalization.
rubric.example: Take a simple random sample of days from the population of interest. Observational data also cannot show causation.
